title: Business Loans for Sole Proprietors in Canada: What Lenders Check
excerpt: Yes, a sole proprietor can get a business loan in Canada. Lenders review your personal credit, tax returns and bank statements. Here is what to prepare and which products fit.
content:
Yes. A sole proprietor can get a business loan in Canada, but the lender treats you and your business as one borrower. That means your personal credit, your tax returns and your net income carry most of the weight. Business history helps, but it rarely replaces them.

This guide explains what lenders check, which products fit a sole proprietorship, and what to prepare before you apply.

Short answer

Sole proprietors can qualify for equipment financing, term loans, merchant cash advances and invoice factoring. Expect lenders to review your personal credit score, your last two years of tax filings and recent bank statements. You are personally responsible for the debt, so borrow only an amount the business can repay.

Can a sole proprietor get a business loan in Canada?

Yes, and many do. A sole proprietorship is not a separate legal entity, so there is no company credit file to review. The lender reads your file instead.

That cuts both ways. You can apply without incorporating, and a short business history is less of a barrier when your personal finances are strong. But a thin or damaged personal credit file affects the whole application.

What do lenders look at for a sole proprietorship?

Lenders look at four things: your personal credit, your net business income, your cash flow and the purpose of the loan. They want proof that the business earns enough to cover the payments on top of your own living costs.

Sole proprietors report business income on their personal tax return using the CRA's Form T2125, Statement of Business or Professional Activities. Lenders often compare the net income on that form with your bank deposits.

Watch this

Large tax deductions lower your net income on paper. A lender that qualifies you on net income sees the smaller number, even if the business has strong sales.

Time in business matters too. Requirements differ by lender and product, so there is no single minimum. A quick check with the True North loan estimator shows which options you are likely to match.

Which business loans fit a sole proprietor?

The best fit depends on what you are paying for and how your income arrives. The table below compares the four main products on how they work for a sole proprietorship.

Equipment financingTrucks, tools, ovens, machinesThe equipment itself as security

If cost is your main concern, read how business loan fees change the real price before you compare offers. Factor-rate products in particular should be converted to an APR first.

What documents does a sole proprietor need?

Have your tax and banking records ready before you apply. Complete files move faster, and missing items are the most common cause of delays.

  • Government-issued photo ID
  • Your last two personal tax returns, including Form T2125, and Notices of Assessment
  • Three to six months of business bank statements
  • A void cheque or banking details for the business account
  • Your business registration or licence, where one applies
  • Quotes or invoices for any equipment you plan to buy

Our full document checklist covers what else lenders may ask for.

Will I have to sign a personal guarantee?

For a sole proprietor, the question is slightly different: you are already personally liable. With no separate company, the debt is yours, and your personal assets can be pursued if the business cannot pay.

Some lenders still ask for a signed guarantee or security on top of that. Read what a personal guarantee really commits you to before you sign.

Should I incorporate before applying?

Not necessarily. Incorporating can separate some business debts from your personal assets, but lenders often still ask the owner to guarantee a small company's loan. It also adds accounting and filing costs, and a new corporation starts with no credit history of its own.

Talk to an accountant or lawyer about tax and liability before you decide. Do not incorporate only to qualify for a single loan.

What mistakes make sole proprietor applications fail?

Most declines trace back to a few preventable problems. Fix these first.

  • Mixing personal and business money. One account for everything makes revenue hard to prove.
  • Ignoring your credit report. Errors and high card balances can sink an otherwise good file.
  • Applying to many lenders separately. Repeated hard credit checks can lower your score.
  • Borrowing more than cash flow supports. You carry the repayment personally.

If your credit needs work, start with how to build business credit in Canada. If you are early in your journey, see startup business loan options.

Frequently asked questions

Can a sole proprietor get a business loan with bad credit?

Sometimes. Options such as merchant cash advances and invoice factoring lean less on credit, but they usually cost more. Compare the total cost, not only the monthly payment.

Do I need a business bank account as a sole proprietor?

It is not a legal requirement, but lenders strongly prefer one. A separate account makes your revenue easier to verify.

Can I get equipment financing as a sole proprietor?

Yes. The equipment usually serves as security, so approval depends partly on its value as well as your credit and income.

Will applying hurt my credit score?

It depends on the lender. A soft check does not affect your score, while a hard inquiry can. True North starts with a soft credit check to show your options.

Is a sole proprietor loan a personal loan or a business loan?

It is a business loan, but because you and the business are the same legal person, you are personally liable for repayment.

Sources
